summary: Lists requirements for a One-way Active Measurement Protocol. With good time sources, networks can measure one-way delay and loss precisely, and an interoperable protocol is needed. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3763 sets out what a common protocol for measuring one-way delay and loss has to do before anyone writes it. It says the protocol must keep all the raw measurement data so that any statistic can be worked out afterwards, must split the job in two, one protocol for the test packets and one for setting up and collecting the sessions, and must limit the kinds of packet it is willing to send.

subtitle: What a common one-way measurement protocol has to do before it can be written

tldr.problem: One-way delay and one-way loss can be measured accurately now that affordable time sources exist, but the measurement platforms that do it do not interoperate, so results cannot be compared across networks.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists what such a protocol must do: measure one-way characteristics while keeping all the raw data for later analysis, support Poisson streams, separate the protocol that carries the test packets from the protocol that sets up sessions, and restrict the packet types it will send.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document. The protocol itself, with its IANA registrations, is a separate specification, and the document is explicit about that.

facts.label: Packet types required
facts.value: A given DSCP or a given PHB ID

facts.label: Measured characteristics
facts.value: Loss, median delay, mean delay, jitter and the 90th percentile of delay

today: RFC 3763 is an Informational memo published in April 2004, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document: the protocol specification itself, with the IANA registrations, is a separate document.

sections.title: Why a Common Measurement Protocol
sections.content:
With the growing availability of good time sources at network nodes, it becomes increasingly possible to measure one-way IP performance metrics with high precision. To do so in an interoperable manner, a common protocol is required.

The IETF IP Performance Metrics working group has proposed standards track metrics for one-way packet delay and for loss across Internet paths. Although several measurement platforms now implement the collection of these metrics, there is no standard for interoperability. The requirements document is aimed at defining a protocol that lets users take measurements with devices from different vendors at both ends and get meaningful results.

With the increasingly wide availability of affordable global positioning system and CDMA based time sources, hosts increasingly have time sources that let them stamp packets with accuracies substantially better than the delays seen on the Internet, either directly or through their proximity to primary time servers. The authors hope that standardising a technique for collecting these measurements will create an environment where the metrics can be collected across a far broader mesh of Internet paths than is currently possible. One particularly compelling vision is of widespread deployment of open one-way active measurement beacons that would make measurements of one-way delay as commonplace as measurements of round-trip time are today using ICMP-based tools like ping. Even without very accurate timestamps one can measure characteristics such as loss with a quality acceptable for many practical purposes, such as network operations.

To support interoperability between alternative implementations and make possible a world where one-way ping could become commonplace, a standard is required that specifies how test streams are initiated, how test packets are exchanged, and how test results are retrieved.
sections.plainLanguage: Timing a packet one way needs good clocks at both ends, and good clocks are now cheap. What is missing is a common way for the two ends to agree what to send and how to collect the results, so that measurements from different networks can be compared.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol should provide the ability to measure, record and distribute the results of measurements of one-way singleton network characteristics, such as the characteristics defined in the one-way delay and one-way loss metrics. Result reporting, sampling and time stamps are to be within the framework of the IP Performance Metrics framework.

It should be possible to measure arbitrary one-way singleton characteristics, such as loss, median delay, mean delay, jitter or the 90th percentile of delay. This is achieved by keeping all the raw data for post-processing by the final data consumer. Since the delay and loss metrics standardise metrics based on Poisson sampling processes, Poisson streams must be supported by the protocol.

Non-singleton characteristics, such as those related to trains of packets and back-to-back tuples, and application traffic simulation need not be addressed, although they may be addressed if they are considered practical and not in contradiction to other design goals.

On keeping data for post-processing, the protocols should not necessitate any required post-processing. This does not apply to implementation details such as converting timestamps from ticks since midnight into a canonical form or applying calibration constants, which should naturally be hidden. All the data obtained during a measurement session should be available after the session is finished if the data consumer wants it, so that various characteristics can be computed from the raw data using arbitrary algorithms.

A means to distribute measurement results, between hosts taking part in a measurement session and beyond, should be provided. Since there can be a wide variety of scenarios for where the final data destination should be, these should be invoked separately from measurement requests, so that the receiver does not have to send the results to the sender automatically, since it may be the receiver or a third host that is the ultimate destination. At the same time, the ability to transfer results directly to their destination, without need for potentially large intermediate transfers, should be provided.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules shape the protocol. Keep everything, so that any statistic can be computed later, and keep the sending of results separate from the request to measure, so that the results can go somewhere other than back to the sender.

sections.title: Two Protocols Instead of One
sections.content:
Measurement session setup and the actual measurement session are different tasks, require different levels of functionality, flexibility and implementation effort, and may need to run over different transport protocols. There should therefore exist two protocols: one for conducting the actual measurement session, called OWAMP-Test, and another for session setup, teardown, confirmation and retrieval, called OWAMP-Control.

It should be possible to use devices that support only OWAMP-Test and not OWAMP-Control to conduct measurement sessions, since such devices will necessarily support one form of session setup protocol or the other, but it does not have to be known to external parties. OWAMP-Control thus becomes a common protocol for different administrative domains, which may or may not use it for session setup internally.

The test protocol needs to be implemented on all measurement nodes, so it should be lightweight and easy to implement, suitable for implementation on a wide range of measurement nodes, and allow UDP as the transport protocol, because the protocol needs to measure individual packet delivery times and has to run on various machines. It should support varying packet sizes and network services such as DSCP marking, and be as simple as possible but no simpler than necessary, with a packet format that includes only universally meaningful fields and the minimum number of them. If practical, it should be possible to generate test packets small enough that each fits inside a single ATM cell once encapsulated. The data needed to calculate experimental errors on the final result should be included in every test packet.

The control protocol needs to provide the capability to authenticate peers to each other using a common authentication method that does not require building any new authentication infrastructure, such as a user ID and a shared secret; to schedule zero or more test sessions, which do not have to be between the peers of the control conversation; to start test sessions simultaneously or at pre-scheduled per-session times; to retrieve test session results, including sessions scheduled in the current and in other control sessions; and to confirm graceful completion of sessions and allow either side to abort a session prematurely. The control design should not preclude the ability to record extended periods of loss, and should always let peers distinguish between network failures and peer failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is split in two on purpose. The packets that carry the measurement have to be tiny and fast, and they run on every measuring device; the business of arranging and collecting the sessions is a separate, more capable protocol that runs between the controllers.

sections.title: How Much of the Packet Space Is Allowed
sections.content:
Since the notion of a packet of type P from the IP Performance Metrics framework does not always imply a precise definition of packet type, some decisions narrowing the scope of possible packet types have to be made at the measurement protocol design stage. Measuring with packets of certain types, while feasible in more closed settings than those implied by OWAMP, becomes very hard in an open inter-domain fashion, for example measurements with packets with a broken IP checksum or particular loose source routing options.

Very general packet type specification could result in several problems. Many test speakers will be general purpose computers with a multitasking operating system and a socket interface, and these will inevitably have higher losses when listening to raw network traffic, since raw sockets induce a higher loss rate than one would have with UDP measurements. It is not at all clear, short of standardizing tcpdump syntax, how to describe formally the filter that a receiver should use to listen for test traffic. Suppose the identity of an authenticated user is compromised: the attacker could use it to run TCP sessions to the rlogin port of machines around servers that trust this user in order to perform measurements, or to send spam, so the ability to perform measurements would be transformed into an ability to generate arbitrary traffic on behalf of all the senders a control server controls. Carefully crafted packets could cause disruption to some link-layer protocols, and implementors cannot know what to disallow, because scrambling differs for different link-layer technologies.

Allowing one to ask a measurement server to generate arbitrary packets becomes an unmanageable security hole and a formidable specification and implementation hurdle. For these reasons, OWAMP is only required to support a small subspace of the whole packet type space: it should be possible to conduct measurements with a given Differentiated Services Codepoint or a given Per Hop Behavior Identification Code.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting a remote user choose any kind of packet to send would be an open door: raw sockets lose packets, filters cannot be described, and a stolen account could be used to send anything at all. So the protocol only has to handle two choices, the traffic class marking and the per-hop behaviour.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content: Some measurement architecture designs have inherent scalability problems, for example a full mesh of always-on measurements among N measurement nodes requires resources growing with the square of N, such as storage space and link capacity. OWAMP itself should not exaggerate that problem or make it impossible, where it is in principle possible, to design other architectures that are free of scalability deficiencies. It is the protocol user's responsibility to decide how to use the protocol and which measurements to conduct.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is not the thing that makes a large measurement programme expensive; the architecture is. The document leaves the choice of architecture to the people running it.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Peers should be able to authenticate to each other using a user ID and a shared secret. It should be infeasible for any external party without knowledge of the shared secret to obtain information about it by observing, initiating or modifying protocol transactions, and it should also be infeasible for such a party to use information obtained in that way to impersonate valid users. Authorisation shall normally be performed on the basis of the authenticated identity, such as a username, and the specification shall require all implementations to support such a mode of authorisation. Different identities, or classes of identities, can have different testing privileges, and the use of authorisation to reach specific policy decisions, such as whether to allow a specific test with a specific source and destination and a given test send schedule, is up to the users.

The design should make it possible to run sessions in which it would be very difficult for an intermediate party to make results appear better than they would be without interference. This is different from cryptographic assurance of data integrity, because results can be manipulated without changing any data in the packets: if test packets are easy to identify, for example because they all arrive at a well-known port number, an intermediate party might place that traffic into a priority queue at a congested link, so that the measurement appears better than what other traffic would experience. It should therefore not be easy for intermediate parties to identify test packets. Confidentiality should hold so that an outside party without the shared secret cannot learn what is exchanged over the control stream, and the document recognises that some information will inevitably leak from the mere fact of communication and from the presence and timing of concurrent and subsequent test traffic.

For integrity, a facility must be provided to authenticate each control message, its attribution to a given session, and its exact placement in the sequence of control exchanges, and to authenticate each test message and its attribution to a specific session so that modifications of test messages can be detected. This must be possible without encrypting the timestamps themselves, in which case the security properties hold only when an attacker cannot observe valid traffic between the sender and the receiver.

On replay attacks, the control protocol must be resistant to any replay attacks. The test protocol, on the other hand, is a protocol for network measurement, and packet duplication is one of the attributes of networks, so it has to be suitable for measuring duplication. That makes it vulnerable to attacks that involve replaying a recent packet, and for the recipient it is impossible to determine whether the duplication is malicious or naturally occurring. The test protocol should therefore measure all duplication, malicious or otherwise, and should measure the network as it was, even though the data may be sanitised later in processing: some sanity checks should be performed by the receiving side immediately.

The protocol must support varying degrees of security mode, considering confidentiality, data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection. There should be a mode in which all security mechanisms are enabled and the objectives are realised as fully as possible, called encrypted mode. Because timestamp encryption takes a certain amount of time, which may be hard to predict on some devices with a time-sharing operating system, there should be a similar mode in which timestamps are not encrypted, keeping all the security properties of encrypted mode that can be retained without it, called authenticated mode. There should also be a completely open mode in which no cryptographic security mechanisms are used, called unauthenticated mode, in which mandatory mechanisms must prevent the protocol being used for network capacity starvation denial-of-service attacks, for example by only sending test data back to the client that requested it with a request delivered over a TCP connection, and must prevent a worm from using the protocol to send test data to a very large number of hosts in a short time, for example by ensuring that open mode requests can only be made by humans and by rate-limiting their acceptance.
sections.plainLanguage: The security rules are set out as three modes. The strictest encrypts everything, the middle one encrypts everything but the timestamps, and the open one relies on rate limits so that the protocol cannot be used to flood a network. The document also insists that test packets should be hard to pick out of ordinary traffic, so that nobody can give them preferential treatment on the way.

UDP, so that individual packet delivery times can be measured

items.title: Encrypted mode
items.text: All security mechanisms are enabled and the security objectives are realised to the fullest extent possible.

items.title: Authenticated mode
items.text: Like encrypted mode, but timestamps are not encrypted. All the other security properties are kept, which matters on devices where encrypting timestamps is slow.

items.title: Unauthenticated mode
items.text: No cryptographic security mechanisms are used, but mandatory rules prevent capacity starvation and stop a worm from using the protocol to flood many hosts.
